newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac condemns plan to legalise French immigrants.
newsitem.headline: Chirac condemns plan to legalise French immigrants.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac, in a clear attack on the Socialist-led government, criticised on Monday moves to relax immigration laws, saying to do so would encourage more illegal immigration.

"It would be an encouragement (to illegal immigrants). Its consequences would be that people elsewhere would say to themselves: 'We might as well go to France because we'll be able to muddle through and stay there whatever happens.'

"The employment and social situation does not allow our country to do this...and it would feed those xenophobic and racist reactions which I hate," Chirac said in a live Bastille Day television interview.

Chirac was commenting on Socialist government plans to legalise up to 40,000 immigrants, many of them black Africans, who have been in legal limbo since the previous centre-right governments passed more restrictive legislation.
Some have overstayed visas or cannot be expelled because they have children born in France and entitled to citizenship.

Chirac's comments follow years of controversy over immigration which have fuelled the electoral rise of Jean-Marie Le Pen's extreme-rightist National Front party. Chirac vowed in the interview to fight the right-wing group.

Chirac said he absolutely rejected racism, anti-semitism and xenophobia but added: "One should not listen solely to one's heart. One should also use one's head and try and see where our nation's interest lies."

He said millions of legal foreign residents were mostly opposed to allowing open-door immigration because "they are terrified at the rejection it would provoke, from which they would be first to suffer".

There are about four million foreign nationals legally resident in France and they have more than two million French-born children who automatically qualify for French citizenship. Up to a million more foreign nationals may be in France illegally.

France has traditionally received waves of foreign immigrants in the past, mostly Italians, Spaniards, Poles and Portuguese, and one in every seven French people now has at least one foreign-born grandparent.

The successful integration of past waves of immigrants has been attributed to the fact they came from other European countries and arrived at times of economic boom when the country needed more labour.
Unemployment today hits more than 12 percent of the French and over half the latest immigrants hail from the third world, including Moslem north or west African states.
A Bastille Day parade in the south France port of Toulon was marked by clashes between anti-racist militants and National Front members, eyewitnesses said.

Toulon's mayor is from the anti-immigration Front and the witnesses said municipal police backed the rightists in the scuffles. There were no immediate reports of serious injuries or arrests were made.
Le Pen was reported present on the reviewing stand when the incidents took place.
